Are there discrete random variables X, Y where the E(X) and E(Y) are finite but E(X + Y) is undefined or infinite?
This question targets a subtle edge case in probability theory.
It asks whether two discrete random variables can have finite expectations.
It also asks whether their sum can have undefined expectation.
The issue concerns how expectations are extended to sums.
A finite expectation requires summability of the distribution.
For a single discrete variable, that is easy to check.
For a sum, the situation is governed by linearity.
The variables individually behave well.
Their combined distribution must also behave well.
The cancellation argument is the key intuition here.
Positive and negative parts must each stay finite.
If both parts diverge, the expectation fails to exist.
The finite expectations of the variables are actually enough.
One must examine the absolute integrability of the sum.
The question is essentially about integrability of random variables.
In measure theory, summability corresponds to integrability.
The finite mean of each variable implies integrability individually.
It automatically guarantees that the sum is integrable.
The sum is integrable if its absolute value has finite mean.
This condition follows from the triangle inequality.
One cannot construct a counterexample with symmetric divergent tails.
The answer to the reference question is no, because the finite absolute integrability of each discrete random variable ensures that their sum remains integrable in an extremely simple, transparent, and mathematically clear way beneath the surface.
